studyAreas.name: Middle Ganga plain, Bihar
labelSources: Sen1Floods11 (contains an India event; exact site to be VERIFIED at ingestion, Phase 2)
studyAreas.selectionRationale: Leading candidate because Sen1Floods11 reportedly includes an India flood event in the Ganga plain, which would place hand-labelled Sentinel-1 water masks inside the target region. That resolves the single hardest problem in the project -- ground truth. Terrain is flat, so SAR backscatter is not confounded by slope or layover, giving the cleanest possible flood signal. Flooding recurs annually during the monsoon, so multiple independent events are available for temporal validation. Exposure is high and rural, which complements the urban Mumbai case.
studyAreas.notes: VERIFY IN PHASE 2 before relying on this: list the actual event codes in the downloaded Sen1Floods11 metadata and confirm both the presence and the exact footprint of the India site. Do not write "includes India" in the report until the file listing says so.

studyAreas.name: Mumbai Metropolitan Region
labelSources: None dense enough for supervised training -- transfer target only
studyAreas.selectionRationale: Selected as a deliberate stress case rather than a training region. SAR flood detection is known to degrade badly in dense urban settings, where double-bounce between buildings and standing water *raises* backscatter instead of lowering it, inverting the physical signal the model relies on. Applying a model trained on rural Bihar to Mumbai and quantifying the drop is a reportable domain-transfer result, not a failure. Annual monsoon flooding, very high exposure, and cyclone-adjacent coastline. This is the evaluation target for contribution C3.
studyAreas.notes: Expect poor IoU here relative to rural AOIs. That is the finding, and it must be reported rather than tuned away.

studyAreas.name: Brahmaputra valley, Assam
studyAreas.selectionRationale: Highest flood recurrence in India and excellent Sentinel-1 coverage, with large, radiometrically clean water bodies. Included as a third AOI if the compute budget allows, primarily to test spatial generalisation across river systems with different channel morphology.

studyAreas.name: Periyar and Chalakudy basins, Kerala
labelSources: Copernicus EMS activations for the August 2018 Kerala floods (activation code NOT yet confirmed)
studyAreas.selectionRationale: Well-documented, internationally mapped 2018 flood event with independent reference delineations. Steep terrain makes it the hardest SAR case of the Indian AOIs -- layover, shadow and slope-driven false negatives -- which makes it a useful adversarial test rather than a training region.
studyAreas.notes: NO VERIFIED EVENT ENTRY. The August 2018 Kerala flood is real and heavily studied, but the Copernicus EMS activation code widely cited for it in secondary sources (EMSR298) belongs to forest fires in central Sweden, July 2018. Rather than record a code that does not check out, this AOI carries no `events` entry until the correct activation is confirmed against the EMS activation list directly. The peer-reviewed SAR inundation studies of this event remain usable as reference literature.

studyAreas.name: Koshi and Madhesh Terai, Nepal
labelSources: UNOSAT satellite-detected water extent products, Sentinel-1, September-October 2024
studyAreas.selectionRationale: A cross-border transfer target that holds the physiography fixed while changing the country. The Koshi Terai is the same Ganga-system alluvial plain as the Bihar AOI -- the Koshi crosses directly from here into Bihar -- so a model trained in Bihar and evaluated here is tested on a genuinely unseen region without confounding the result with a change of terrain regime. That isolates geographic and label-provenance transfer from the terrain and urban effects that Kerala and Mumbai probe. It also has independent delineations produced by a different organisation using a different method, which is a stronger check than re-using the training dataset's own labels.
studyAreas.notes: A second, much more recent Nepal activation exists (Copernicus EMS "Flood in Nepal", northern Nepal, around Syapru Besi) covering building damage. It is not recorded as an event here because its imagery and products have not been checked to the same standard. Add it only after the same three checks pass.

events.name: Nepal floods, late September 2024
events.verificationNote: Checked 2026-09-26. Rainfall between 27 and 28 September 2024 was the heaviest recorded since Nepal's modern hydrological monitoring began in 1970, with nine Kathmandu Valley stations at unprecedented levels. UNOSAT published a satellite-detected water extent product for Koshi and Madhesh Provinces from a Sentinel-1 acquisition on 27 September 2024, distributed via ReliefWeb, and maintains a Sentinel-1 flood monitoring dashboard for Nepal. Copernicus GloFAS carries an independent account of the same event. Sensor, acquisition date and retrievable products all confirmed. UNOSAT's own reported areas and exposure counts are deliberately not copied into this file -- they are reference values for validation, not SAT-AI outputs, and a figure stored here is one refactor away from being rendered as a result. UNOSAT additionally cautions that SAR-derived extent underestimates standing water under dense vegetation and in built-up areas, which applies to any comparison made against these products.

studyAreas.name: Mahanadi delta and Odisha coast
labelSources: Copernicus EMS EMSR357 delineation products, Odisha Coast, May 2019
studyAreas.selectionRationale: The only AOI in the study whose dominant hazard is cyclonic rather than fluvial, and the one that exercises the exposure-along-a-track path of the risk engine rather than its flood path. The Odisha coast takes the most intense landfalls on the Indian east coast and has an unusually complete public record: best-track data from IBTrACS, and independent post-landfall delineations from a European rapid-mapping activation. It is a transfer target, not a training region -- SAT-AI does not forecast cyclone tracks and this AOI is not an attempt to start.
studyAreas.notes: Cyclone scope for this AOI is exposure and extreme-weather indices over an observed or supplied track. Track forecasting requires assimilated observations and numerical weather prediction, which IMD operates and SAT-AI does not.

events.name: Tropical Cyclone Fani landfall, Odisha
events.verificationNote: Checked 2026-09-26. Copernicus EMS activation EMSR357, "Tropical Cyclone Fani in Eastern India". Fani made landfall on 3 May 2019 between Brahmagiri village and Puri, Odisha, as a Category 4 system with maximum sustained winds around 240 km/h -- the most intense tropical cyclone to make landfall in India in the preceding twenty years. Delineation products for the Odisha Coast area of interest were produced from TerraSAR-X and COSMO-SkyMed imagery acquired on 4 and 5 May 2019. Activation code, landfall date, location and sensors all confirmed against the EMS activation page and the Copernicus newsroom. The flooded-area figure published in the overview map is a Copernicus EMS result and is deliberately not stored here.

studyAreas.name: Kumaon hills, Uttarakhand
studyAreas.selectionRationale: The wildfire AOI. Chir pine forest across the Kumaon hills burns nearly every pre-monsoon season, and NASA FIRMS provides continuous VIIRS and MODIS active-fire detections over it, which is the one hazard stream in this project that is a direct instrument observation rather than a model output. That makes it the cleanest place to demonstrate the observation-versus-model distinction the provenance contract is built around: a thermal anomaly is a measurement at overpass time, a fire-danger index is not.
studyAreas.notes: NO VERIFIED EVENT. Uttarakhand's recurrent forest fires are well documented, but no specific burn has yet been checked to the standard the `events` block requires -- a named sensor, a confirmed acquisition and a retrievable product. FIRMS detections must be queried for an actual date window and bounding box before an event is recorded here. Until then this AOI supports fire-danger indices and FIRMS ingestion, and the interface shows no burned-area analysis for it. `label_sources` is empty on purpose: there is no burn-severity ground truth here, so any dNBR product over this AOI is unvalidated and must be labelled as such.
